questions.stem: Daniel, 32, is on the couch at his GP with 12 hours of periumbilical pain, fever and vomiting. You have found tenderness and guarding in the right iliac fossa. You now want to test for Rovsing's sign and tell the examiner what you are doing. How do you elicit it, and what is a positive result?
options: Extend his right hip while he lies on his left side; right iliac fossa pain increases
Press deeply in the left iliac fossa; he feels the pain in the right iliac fossa
Flex his right hip and knee, then rotate internally; he feels pain in the hypogastrium
Press slowly in the right iliac fossa, then let go suddenly; the pain is worse on release
questions.why: Rovsing's sign is right iliac fossa pain when you press on the left iliac fossa. Pressing there shifts gas and bowel and moves the inflamed peritoneum on the right, so pain referred to the RIF points to appendicitis.
notes: This is the psoas sign. It suggests a retrocaecal appendix lying on the iliopsoas, not Rovsing's sign.
This is the obturator sign. It suggests a pelvic appendix lying against obturator internus.
This is rebound tenderness, a sign of peritonism. It is not Rovsing's sign, and many examiners prefer gentle percussion because it hurts less.

questions.stem: Daniel, 32, has been transferred to ED and the surgeons plan a laparoscopic appendicectomy. He weighs 78 kg. As a child he got an itchy rash a few days into a course of amoxicillin, with no swelling or breathing trouble. What is the most appropriate pre-incision antibiotic prophylaxis?
options: Vancomycin IV plus metronidazole IV, because all beta-lactams must be avoided
Ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV plus metronidazole 500 mg IV, because cephalosporins cross-react
Cefazolin 2 g IV plus metronidazole 500 mg IV, as his allergy history is low risk
Amoxicillin–clavulanate IV after premedication with an oral antihistamine
questions.why: eTG prophylaxis for appendicectomy is cefazolin 2 g IV plus metronidazole 500 mg IV. A non-severe delayed rash to a penicillin is low risk, and cefazolin, whose side chain is unlike amoxicillin's, can be given safely.
notes: Avoiding every beta-lactam is only needed after a severe reaction (such as anaphylaxis or a severe skin reaction). Using vancomycin without reason gives worse cover and drives resistance.
Cross-reactivity between penicillins and cefazolin is very low. Ciprofloxacin is not the standard prophylaxis and adds no benefit here.
Premedicating with an antihistamine does not make re-exposure safe. Restarting a penicillin is done by a formal oral challenge, not around emergency surgery.

questions.stem: Daniel, 32, says his pain started 12 hours ago as a dull, vague ache around the umbilicus. On examination he now has peritonism in the right iliac fossa. What best explains why early appendicitis is felt around the umbilicus?
options: Irritation of the parietal peritoneum, which has somatic innervation from T12 and L1 roots
Referred pain via the phrenic nerve from irritated peritoneum under the diaphragm
Direct spread of inflammation to the muscles of the periumbilical abdominal wall
Stretching of the appendix wall, sensed by visceral afferents entering the cord at T10
questions.why: The appendix is a midgut structure. When it swells, visceral afferents enter the spinal cord at about T10 and the pain is referred, poorly localised, to the T10 dermatome around the umbilicus. It localises to the right iliac fossa later, once the somatic parietal peritoneum is inflamed.
notes: Parietal peritoneal irritation causes the later, well-localised pain in the right iliac fossa, not the early vague periumbilical ache.
Phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) irritation is referred to the shoulder tip, not the umbilicus.
The abdominal wall is not involved early. If it were, the pain would be sharp and well localised, not vague.

questions.stem: Examining Daniel, 32, you find tenderness that is maximal at McBurney's point, with guarding and rebound. The examiner asks you to show exactly where this point is on the surface of his abdomen. Where is McBurney's point?
options: One-third of the way along a line from the right ASIS to the umbilicus
Midpoint of a line joining the right ASIS to the umbilicus
Midpoint of the right inguinal ligament, just above the femoral pulse
Where the right lateral rectus border meets the costal margin (9th costal cartilage)
questions.why: McBurney's point lies one-third of the way from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. It marks the usual position of the base of the appendix, where the taeniae coli meet on the caecum.
notes: The midpoint is too far medial. McBurney's point is closer to the ASIS, one-third of the way along the line.
The midpoint of the inguinal ligament overlies the femoral vessels, deep ring and hernial region, not the appendix base.
This is the surface marking of the gallbladder fundus, where Murphy's sign is tested.
